title: 20-year-old Michigan man killed by possible lightning strike in Florida
text:
A 20-year-old Michigan man who had moved to Central Florida just days earlier to begin the Disney College Program was killed in an apparent lightning strike while on a walking path, authorities and his family said.
Matthew Eric Jenkins of Shelby Township, Michigan, was found unresponsive Tuesday evening on a walking path behind a hotel in Celebration, according to the Osceola County Sheriff's Office.
Jenkins' father told WESH-TV his son had moved to Central Florida last week to begin the internship program at Walt Disney World.
AMERICAN TOURIST KILLED BY LIGHTNING WHILE HIKING SICILY'S MOUNT ETNA
Deputies were called to the path in the 700 block of Bloom Street at about 6:25 p.m. Investigators said lightning had struck nearby.
Spyro Betz, who had been walking nearby before reaching his car, told FOX35 Orlando he heard a powerful crack of lightning.
"I heard the big crack of lightning that was like right overhead," Betz said.
He initially thought it had struck a building.
"When I heard the lightning strike, I expected it hit the building or something like that or hit the hotel. I didn't expect it to hit a person," Betz said.
Felipe Costa told WESH-TV he ran toward the path after hearing the lightning and found Jenkins on the ground.
LIGHTNING STRIKE TURNS 100-FOOT DINOSAUR INTO RAGING FIREBALL, STUNNING ONLOOKERS
"As soon as I heard that, I started running, and I came over here [where it happened]. That's when I saw the man," Costa said.
A woman joined Costa and began performing CPR while they waited for first responders.
Jenkins was taken to AdventHealth Celebration, where he was pronounced dead.
Jenkins' father told the outlet that the family was grateful to everyone who tried to help his son.

The sheriff's office said detectives are awaiting the medical examiner's determination of Jenkins' official cause of death.

title: NTSB reveals if crew survived Amazon cargo jet disaster as it shares details about victims
text:
Federal regulators said the two crew members aboard the Amazon cargo jet that crashed at Miami International Airport on Sunday survived the accident.
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) provided the update during a Sunday press conference after officials said the cargo plane overran the runway and caught fire while landing. The crash killed five people and injured five others, authorities said Sunday.
The jet collided with two vehicles carrying at least eight occupants, according to NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy.
Seven of the victims were in a van that was struck and "torn apart" on airport grounds, Homendy said. The 2012 white Ford Econoline van was owned by Ocean Service Corporation, a contract cleaning company that provides services for airlines, she said.
AMAZON CARGO PLANE OVERRUNS MIAMI AIRPORT RUNWAY AND STRIKES 'MULTIPLE' VEHICLES; 5 DEAD, 5 INJURED
The NTSB said the aircraft then crashed through the airport perimeter and struck a civilian vehicle, a Toyota Corolla Cross LE, that was traveling on Northwest 67th Avenue.
Homendy said investigators observed what appeared to be deployed airbags in the vehicles as they surveyed the crash site.
"You can see components from vehicles, both passenger vehicles and the aircraft itself," Homendy said.
The jet then "continued into the grass and impacted another fence line, which separated an area where Tesla robotaxis were stationed," Homendy said.
In total, the jet reportedly traveled 1,300 feet beyond the paved surface.
Homendy said the wreckage was "extensive," noting that the crash damaged airport navigational aids and equipment, while fencing was ripped apart throughout the area.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES
Officials said the Boeing 767 had completed two other flights before crashing in Miami, where its operator, 21 Air LLC, is based.
The aircraft traveled from Cincinnati to Miami, then from Miami to San Juan, Puerto Rico, before returning to Miami, Homendy said.
NTSB investigators have recovered the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder, which they planned to examine.

Homendy described the crash site as "devastating," saying wreckage was scattered throughout the area.
"I would describe it in one word, devastating, utter devastation," she said.
"I mean, you can see on the paved surface, tire marks that continue through the grass. There's debris everywhere."

title: Dramatic video captures floodwaters bursting through glass doors of college students’ home
text:
Video captured the tense moment when several feet-high floodwaters suddenly burst through the glass doors of an off-campus student home, sending a door panel flying across the room as water rushed inside and inundated the lower level.
The incident happened Aug. 27 after severe storms brought major flash flooding to Glassboro, New Jersey, as Rowan University students were preparing to move into housing ahead of the September start of the school year.
Tommy Scirrotto, a resident, said the flooding caused extensive damage to four bedrooms on the lower level of the home, according to a GoFundMe post.
"The storms in Glassboro, Nj claimed the entirety of the lower level at our home. 4 bedrooms completely flooded, resulting in a huge amount of damage," Scirrotto said.
HURRICANE KATRINA TAUGHT ME HOW TO PREPARE FOR ANY STORM
At the start of the video, about an inch of water had already seeped into the lower level.
As a student approached the doors, several feet of floodwater could be seen building up on the other side, appearing on the verge of breaking through. Towels had also been placed along the base of the French doors in an attempt to keep the water out.
Just as the student said, "This door is gonna break," one of the doors immediately gave way and was sent flying across the room.
DEADLY GRAND CANYON FLOODING KNOCKS OUT CRITICAL WATER LINE AMID RACE TO FIND MISSING HIKERS
In the chaotic moment, water rushed inside, eventually overtaking multiple makeshift barriers made of laundry that appeared to have been used to slow the initial flow of water.
Photos posted on GoFundMe showed furniture, beds and rugs completely submerged in floodwater.

On the same day, Rowan University issued a warning about severe flash-flooding conditions across the region, adding that water had also "infiltrated" the Glassboro campus.
"Several campus buildings have also taken on water," the university said.
"Please exercise caution and stay safe during this severe weather."

title: Fighter jet crashes at air show, killing 2 pilots with thousands of spectators watching
text:
A day at an air show turned fatal Saturday when a Greek air force jet crashed north of Athens as thousands of spectators watched.
Both pilots were killed in the crash at Tanagra Air Force Base, but no civilians were hurt.
The twin-seat Phantom F-4 jet flew into the ground during a low-altitude maneuver just meters above the ground.
EIGHT BELIEVED DEAD AFTER B-52 CRASHES SHORTLY AFTER TAKEOFF FROM EDWARDS AIR FORCE BASE
"The sense of grief is widespread, and our thoughts are with the families of the two pilots we lost," Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said. "It is a reminder of the daily danger faced by Greece’s aviators, who remain on constant standby to protect Greece's skies."
The jet burst into flames on impact, sending up a large plume of black smoke, prompting 11 water-dropping planes and helicopters to assist 85 firefighters in extinguishing the blaze.
11 SKYDIVERS, ONE PILOT KILLED IN MISSOURI PLANE CRASH NEAR AIRPORT
Video of the crash showed a second ball of fire nearby as the plane broke apart.
The bodies of the pilots were eventually recovered.
"We were all stunned. It hadn't been airborne for more than three minutes," an eyewitness told ERT, Greece’s state-owned broadcaster.
The crash happened during the country’s annual Athens Flying Week.
The organizers canceled the rest of the events after the incident, and the area was evacuated.
"It is with deep sadness that I learned of the death of the two officers of the Hellenic Air Force, who lost their lives in the tragic accident that occurred during the air show at Tanagra Air Base," Cyprus' Defense Minister Vasilis Palmas said, adding he had called Nikos Dendias, Greece’s Minister of National Defense.

The air force has declared three days of mourning in the country.

title: Trapped Nepal workers pulled alive from tunnel 9 days after deadly flooding, raising hope for more rescues
text:
Rescue teams in Nepal pulled two workers alive from a hydropower tunnel nine days after catastrophic floods swept through the country, leaving more than 1,000 people dead and thousands more missing.
Nepalese lawmaker Shri Ram Neupane told The Associated Press that searchers first heard men's voices in the tunnel on Friday morning. Images distributed by the Nepal Army showed a rescuer carrying one of the workers on his back while soldiers on either side helped.
The breakthrough has raised hopes that the dozens of others believed to be trapped will be rescued. One of the rescued men said more people are alive inside the tunnel, according to Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet, who said the search is ongoing.
SON REALIZES MISSING AMERICAN DAD WAS IN PATH OF NEPAL DISASTER AFTER WATCHING VIRAL VIDEO
"I can’t explain what we are feeling at the moment. We are just grateful to God," Amir Maharjan, the brother of one of those rescued, told the AP.
Both men were flown to a hospital in Kathmandu, and one of them was in critical condition, the AP reported, citing a statement from the prime minister's office.
Officials identified them as a mechanical foreman and a mechanical supervisor at the Trishuli 3A plant.
TERRIFYING VIDEO CAPTURES PEOPLE FLEEING INCOMING MUDSLIDE AT NEPAL-CHINA BORDER
The AP reported that about 115 people are believed to remain trapped in the Trishuli 3A tunnel alone, citing the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal.
In total, authorities say there are about 900 workers missing from 12 hydropower plants in Nepal, with about 500 of them believed to be trapped in tunnels.
Nepal’s Communication Minister Bikram Timilsina wrote on his Facebook page that officials "are waiting for the rescue of more and more people."
"A heartfelt thank you to everyone who worked tirelessly day and night to rescue two people alive!" Timilsina added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The AP reported that at least 1,287 people have been killed and more than 5,000 remain missing after the Aug. 26 floods, which scientists believe were likely triggered by a glacier collapse.
China said on Wednesday that on the Tibet side of the border, 21 people were killed and 541 are missing.
Nepal's disaster agency chief told Reuters on Friday that the flooding has likely caused at least 387.5 billion Nepalese rupees (about $2.5 billion) in damage to infrastructure and property.
The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

title: Rescuers use ziplines to transport trapped citizens after devastating Nepal floods decimate country's bridges
text:
Rescue workers in Nepal were forced to use cable cars and ziplines to ferry stranded citizens across rivers after August's deadly flood and mudslide wiped out local bridges.
Video shows teams of workers yanking ropes to ferry locals who were stranded on an embankment flanked by a flooded river. In one clip, a pair of people sit in a small box attached to a wire as they're yanked onto a platform across a river in Nuwakot, Nepal.
The rescues come as both Nepal and neighboring China continue to deal with the aftermath of the Aug. 26 mudslide and ensuing floods in Tibet's Gyirong Valley and the Nepal's Trishuli River Valley.
EXPERTS ZERO IN ON LIKELY CAUSE OF DEADLY NEPAL MUDSLIDE, WITH MORE THAN 1,400 MISSING
As of Wednesday, at least 1,114 people have been confirmed dead and nearly 4,000 remain missing in Nepal. Chinese authorities report an additional 16 confirmed dead and at least 541 missing on their side of the border.
Rescuers are still working to search and rescue any potential survivors trapped in a hydropower tunnel in the Rasuwa district.

"In Rasuwagadhi, we think 46 people are trapped in a room-like structure in the tunnel," Amshu Kiran Shahi, a board member of the Nepal Electricity Authority that operates the hydropower plant, told Reuters.
A senior official in President Donald Trump's administration also told Fox News that an additional two Americans made it to safety in Nepal, marking 16 total Americans in the country who made their way to safety.

title: Raging inferno erupts at Bali beachside restaurant party
text:
A beachside party in Bali, Indonesia, erupted into chaos after a balloon reportedly exploded inside a popular restaurant, sparking a raging inferno.
Videos captured flames ripping through the Chez Gado-Gado restaurant in the Seminyak resort area during the incident Sunday, which left an Australian teenager hospitalized with burns, according to 7News.
"There was a 70th birthday, and they had two balloons on their table and a waitress went to light the candle on the birthday cake, but she lit it a bit too close to the balloon," Tara Borelli, a witness from Sydney, told News.com.au. "It popped, then exploded. We felt the heat from the pop."
"I just grabbed my daughter and little cousin and ran straight onto the beach towards the water," Borelli added, describing how the straw roof of the restaurant immediately caught fire and "within minutes" the entire restaurant was ablaze.
ONE TOURIST DEAD AFTER MASSIVE FIRE NEARLY DESTROYS CARIBBEAN RESORT; 1,690 EVACUATED
"It lit up like a firecracker... people were screaming and crying and running around," Paul Cole, another witness, told 9News.
The Badung Fire and Rescue Service said it took more than two hours to put out the flames and there were no casualties, according to The Bali Sun.
First Inspector I Gede Adi Saputra Jaya of the Denpasar Police, citing statements from witnesses at the scene, told reporters Monday that the fire is "strongly suspected" to have started after a balloon "was hit by a candle flame, causing it to explode and catch fire," the website added.
HUNDREDS OF POUNDS OF FIREWORKS EXPLODE, DESTROYING HOMES AND INJURING FIREFIGHTERS
"Initial extinguishing efforts using fire extinguishers by restaurant staff were unsuccessful because the fire had already grown large and spread quickly to the thatched roof," he reportedly said.
One witness told 9News, "There are the balloons, a lot of explosions, explosion and explosion and explosion, it was just, yeah, it was terrible."
"It was just bedlam," added Joe Xuereb, another witness. "As soon as the fire started, people didn’t know what to do."

title: Haitian college student in Ohio dies by apparent suicide after losing TPS status, family says
text:
If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).
A Haitian-born college student in Ohio died in what his family believes to be a suicide after he lost his temporary protected status (TPS) protections amid the Trump administration’s termination of Haiti’s TPS designation.
Pierre Damas Bel, 20, died on Monday as he walked into oncoming traffic after parking his vehicle on the right shoulder of Interstate 70, according to Ohio State Highway Patrol.
"Bel succumbed to fatal injuries at the scene," Ohio State Highway Patrol said in a statement, adding that the incident remains under investigation.
Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican, said Tuesday that Bel's death is a "horrible, horrible tragedy."
SUPREME COURT'S LATEST IMMIGRATION RULING WILL CAUSE AMERICANS TO 'DIE AND SUFFER' ATTORNEY WARNS
"He graduated from high school here," DeWine said. "He was well liked. He was in the junior ROTC. And, I’m told by those that knew him that he had great dreams about what he could do in this country and what he could contribute to this country."
"I think we have to ask ourselves: Is this really good? Is it what we want done to people like this being picked up and facing deportation? Do we want that being done in our name?" he asked.
Bel's father told The Haitian Times that his son was "distraught" after weeks of wearing an ankle monitor. He was among some Haitian immigrants in the Springfield, Ohio, area who have been required by the Department of Homeland Security to wear ankle monitors, after the U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for the administration to end Haiti’s TPS designation, potentially exposing roughly 350,000 Haitian nationals to removal.
"In his last days, I did not recognize him as he was such an energetic kid who loves life, friends and family, and education," Bel's father, Pierre Ronal Bel, said in a statement read by Pastor Carl Ruby.
Bel's father said he was "treated like an animal" after receiving his ankle monitor, according to WSYX.
His father told The Washington Post that Bel left home before 8 a.m. on Monday and called shortly after to tell his father he was not feeling okay mentally.
"I told him, 'Come home so that we can talk?' I had my youngest to take to school. I took him to school," his father said.
But later that morning, police showed up at his home to inform him his son had died.
A month before his death, Bel spoke out about his experience wearing an ankle monitor.
HOUSE REPUBLICAN BREAKS WITH TRUMP, SAYS ENDING HAITIAN TPS RISKS US HEALTHCARE 'CRISIS'
"I came to this country to pursue my education. I didn't come here to commit a crime or hurt anyone," he wrote on social media.
"Yet now I’m walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg, carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation that I never imagined I would experience," he added. "I came here to study, to build my future and to live a better [life,] not to be treated like a criminal. So now, how am I supposed to play college sports with a GPS monitor on my leg?"
Ruby said on Monday that the family believes Bel took his own life as a result of President Donald Trump's immigration agenda that targeted TPS.
"I'm sitting with a family right now whose son threw himself in front of semi truck today after being teased by fellow students at Wright State about his ankle monitor," Ruby wrote on Facebook.
"I wish President Trump could hear the mom's wails. The family wants people to know that this was a suicide, and they want people to know that President Trump, [White House deputy chief of staff] Stephen Miller, and [Homeland Security Secretary] Markwayne Mullin’s inhumane immigration policies made this happen," the pastor continued.
Many of the roughly 15,000 Haitian immigrants in Springfield have lived in the U.S. for years, unable to return to their home country that has faced years of violence, turmoil and extreme poverty.
In a statement to WBTN, ICE said it "does not comment on the cause of death while that investigation is pending, and we will not speculate about unverified claims regarding other individuals."

Bel graduated from high school in May and was set to begin his first semester at Wright State University after being unable to play college soccer at Wittenberg University because of his ankle monitor, the Wittenberg men’s soccer team said in a Facebook post.
"He took 2 trips to Cincinnati and Westerville to plead to the officers to remove the bracelet since he’s a soccer player and he felt embarrassed and humiliated when he’s among his classmates at the University," Bel’s father wrote on X. "Last Friday, August 28, 2026, he told me, 'Dad I felt humiliated. Since they gave uniforms to all my classmates at JROTC their uniform, but except me because of the bracelet.'"
Wright State University President Sue Edwards said the school is "heartbroken by this devastating loss."
"Pierre was an active honors student who was passionate about soccer and was already actively engaged in his classes and the campus community. The University mourns the death of Pierre and extends our deepest condolences to his family, friends and loved ones during this unimaginably difficult time," Edwards said in a statement.

title: 2 Grand Canyon flooding victims photographed on hiking trip in days before deaths
text:
The two victims whose remains were found after flash flooding swept through the Grand Canyon were seen photographed on the same trip prior to the deadly incident.
The families of Texas chiropractor John Giusti, 46, and martial artist Brent Rosenkranz, 42, identified them as the two people whose bodies were recovered, according to Hannah Barricks, a liaison for the families. She told The Associated Press that a third friend, Timothy Smith, 53, went on the trip with them and remains missing as of late Monday.
All three men had ties to Granbury, Texas, and their families said they planned "several days of hiking, camping, fishing and exploring together," the AP also reported. The men spoke to their families Thursday and found their campsite Friday at the bottom of the Grand Canyon, the three families said in a joint statement released earlier Monday through Barricks.
The devastating flash flooding on Saturday, Aug. 29, happened along Bright Angel Creek, which flows into the Colorado River near Phantom Ranch. The area has a set of historic dormitories, a canteen and a campground that is a popular stopover for river rafters and people hiking from one rim of the Grand Canyon to the other.
GRAND CANYON WATER PIPELINE DAMAGED AGAIN AS FLOODING COMPLICATES REPAIRS
Incident Cmdr. Dave Black said searchers used night vision and other equipment to find people who needed rescuing during the deluge. By sunset Saturday, 45 people were rescued, and 37 others were evacuated Sunday.
Rangers referred to the park’s permit system and checked vehicle license plates to track the number of missing people.
"As of right now, they have no reason to believe, from the tips we’ve been through so far, that there’s anybody besides the one" missing person, Black said during a news conference Monday evening.
Hiker Daniel Evans told the AP that it rained several times before the worst 30-minute downpour Saturday afternoon. He had been planning to rest through the hot day and spend the night near the hard-hit Bright Angel Campground area.
Earlier, rangers told him it looked to be safe. Then, as the rain poured, they told him it was time to go. He said he thought of Nepal and the massive floods and landslides that poured down mountain valleys last week.
BELOVED TEXAS CHIROPRACTOR KILLED IN GRAND CANYON FLASH FLOOD
"The entire time it was raining — the entire time I’m going through all this and packing — I’m just keeping my eyes upstream, just praying that a wall of water isn’t coming toward us," Evans said.
Janet Giusti, the wife of John Giusti, wrote on a fundraising page that "John was living out a lifetime dream exploring the majesty of the Grand Canyon when tragedy struck."
"Beyond his practice, he was a man of electric energy and boundless passion — an avid runner, an enthusiast of fast cars, and a massive fan of comic books and legendary heroes," she added. "Yet out of all the titles he carried, his absolute favorite was being a devoted father to his three beautiful girls."
Rosenkranz had posted selfies from the Grand Canyon before the flooding, tagging Giusti and sharing his excitement about the grueling adventure ahead.
"Just arrived at the Grand Canyon. Will be hiking over 31 miles next four days with vertical change of over a mile," Rosenkranz wrote. "Carrying a 40 lb backpack. This should be an adventure!"

Tina Newberry, whose daughter co-owns the ATA Glen Rose martial arts location, said Giusti had been exploring the canyon with fellow "ATA fathers" Rosenkranz and Smith when disaster struck.

title: Grand Canyon water pipeline damaged again as flooding complicates repairs
text:
The one pipeline that supplies water for millions of visitors in the Grand Canyon was badly damaged by flash flooding over the weekend, setting up a complicated repair scenario and disrupting a yearslong project to upgrade the aging line across rugged terrain where helicopters are often needed for even basic maintenance.
Park officials estimate after conducting flyovers that about 40% of the pipeline sustained damage. The 12.5-mile long Transcanyon Waterline has suffered dozens of breaks in recent years. A more than $200 million repair and replacement project was well underway when the floods began.
The long-term impacts on the park’s infrastructure, visitors and year-round residents were not immediately clear.
BELOVED TEXAS CHIROPRACTOR KILLED IN GRAND CANYON FLASH FLOOD, 2 FRIENDS STILL MISSING AFTER HIKE
"We anticipate miles of the pipeline being destroyed," Grand Canyon Deputy Superintendent Brian Drapeaux said.
A full survey of the devastation will not be completed until Tuesday at the earliest.
At least two people died in the floods, and one person remained missing as of Monday night after roughly 80 people were rescued over the weekend, according to officials.
The park stopped overnight accommodations, with officials saying significant water reductions are needed. This includes limiting shower time, turning off the tap while brushing teeth and flushing toilets selectively to protect the limited stored water on the South Rim, where most visitors frequent.
"They have got to keep law enforcement going, they have to keep rescue operations going, backcountry operations, park admin going, the clinic and the campground," longtime river runner and Grand Canyon hiker Tom Martin said, adding that the park has hauled water in tanker trucks in the past.
The pipeline, which was completed in the 1970s, has broken more than 85 times since 2010.
The pipeline moves water from one side of the canyon, down to its base, across a bridge and back up the other side of the rough landscape. Any attempt to fix a break from rock falls or flash floods is precarious and costly and can take time, so fixing the latest damage will be complicated.
The pipeline upgrade project, which began in 2023, took more than a decade to design and fund. The project involves installing helicopter pads, building water treatment facilities and replacing several miles of pipeline. It also seeks to move the water intake for the pipeline further down the canyon to Bright Angel Creek, which would put it closer to Phantom Ranch, a popular lodge at the base of the canyon.
A 2018 evaluation of the project said key infrastructure for the intake would be outside of areas likely to flood.
Officials said even basic decisions proved to be complicated.
For example, the original pipe was aluminum, which is lighter and easier to move into the steep canyon but is more susceptible to breaking. Engineers chose a flex-steel material to balance weight and durability.
Even routine pipeline breaks lead to water restrictions. A decade ago, a hotel on the canyon’s rim that offers luxury dining and highlights its history hosting presidents had to reduce dishwashing and use paper plates and plastic utensils.
In 1995, a nearly monthlong repair on the pipeline required officials to truck in water.
The park had water conservation initiatives in place even before the latest flooding and damage.

text:
A beloved Texas chiropractor and father of three who disappeared during devastating flash flooding at the Grand Canyon has died, his former chiropractic practice announced Monday.
Dr. John Giusti, of Granbury, Texas, had been exploring the Grand Canyon when a flash flood tore through Bright Angel Creek on Aug. 29, turning what his wife described as a "lifetime dream" into tragedy.
"We are heartbroken to make this update. Dr. John was one of the victims of the Grand Canyon flooding," Whipple City Family Chiropractic, where Giusti previously practiced for eight years, announced on Facebook.
"John was a real-life superhero to everyone blessed enough to know him," Janet Giusti wrote in a tribute shared on the fundraiser.

Photos posted to Giusti’s ChiroHabit business page also show him in the Grand Canyon before the flooding began.
Janet remembered her husband as a dedicated chiropractor who "truly lived to treat and heal," but said his most cherished role was being a father.
"Beyond his practice, he was a man of electric energy and boundless passion---an avid runner, an enthusiast of fast cars, and a massive fan of comic books and legendary heroes," she wrote. "Yet out of all the titles he carried, his absolute favorite was being a devoted father to his three beautiful girls."
Janet said her husband was fulfilling a longtime dream when the deadly flood struck.
"John was living out a lifetime dream exploring the majesty of the Grand Canyon when tragedy struck," she wrote. "On August 29, 2026, a sudden flash flood swept through Bright Angel Creek, tragically taking him from us while he was immersed in an adventure he had longed for."
While describing the family's grief as "as vast and profound as the canyon itself," Janet said they were finding some solace in how John spent his final moments.
"We find a small comfort in knowing he spent his final moments surrounded by breathtaking beauty, living life to the fullest," she wrote.
Her tribute ended with a heartbreaking description of the different roles Giusti played in the lives of those around him.
"To the community, he was a gifted healer. To his friends, a powerhouse of life. To his daughters, he was their ultimate hero. To me, he was my whole world," Janet wrote.

The agency is asking anyone who knows of hikers or backpackers who were in the Bright Angel Creek corridor on Aug. 29 or who had a campground reservation there to contact investigators.
Whipple City Family Chiropractic separately announced it was collecting donations at its Greenwich and Cambridge offices and would match the contributions to provide immediate support to the Giusti family.
Giusti practiced chiropractic care for 19 years and was a partner at Whipple City Family Chiropractic in New York for eight years before moving to Granbury in 2020, according to his business biography. He and Janet were raising their three
daughters in Texas.

Giusti was not alone in the canyon when the flooding struck.

Rosenkranz had posted selfies from the Grand Canyon before the flooding, tagging Giusti and sharing his excitement about the grueling adventure ahead.
"Just arrived at the Grand Canyon. Will be hiking over 31 miles next four days with vertical change of over a mile," Rosenkranz wrote. "Carrying a 40 lb backpack. This should be an adventure!"

The Dalai Lama, the highest spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhism, released a message to those affected by the floods in the region.

title: Small plane crashes into shallow water near remote Alaska town, killing all 4 people aboard
text:
A small airplane crashed into shallow waters near a remote coastal town in Alaska on Wednesday, killing all four people on board, according to officials.
The aircraft, a Piper PA-24-260, was heading for an airport in the small town of Seldovia after taking off from Merrill Field Airport in Anchorage when it crashed at around 1:18 p.m., the Alaska Department of Public Safety said in a statement.
Seldovia's airport is about 136 miles southwest of Anchorage.

TWO US ARMY CORPS OF ENGINEERS EMPLOYEES AMONG 8 KILLED IN ALASKA CHARTER PLANE CRASH
A helicopter crew from Anchorage was dispatched to the crash site and other troopers were sent by boat from Anchor Point.

Once the tide level dropped at about 6:30 p.m., troopers were able to retrieve the bodies of the four adult victims from the plane.
The bodies will be sent to the state medical examiner’s office for autopsy. The victims' names will be released once next of kin are notified, according to the Alaska Department of Public Safety.
It remains unclear what may have caused the crash.
The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the crash.

title: Denmark's left-wing PM warns: 'Big enemy has started to grow from within' as Europe faces migrant reckoning
text:
Denmark's left-wing prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, has sent shock waves throughout the European left after recent comments about the Scandinavian nation's — and the continent's — failure to deal with radical Islam among migrant communities.
Her comments come after the mass migration chaos in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, when Frederiksen criticized the actions of Spain's leftist leader, Pedro Sánchez, during a special session on Ceuta in the Danish Parliament.
Responding to a question from a far-left legislator on Denmark’s apparent lack of "solidarity" with Spain against "anti-democratic forces" pressuring Europe, Frederiksen said, "If we talk about undemocratic forces, then Russia is our biggest enemy. The problem is that a big enemy has started to grow from within, and it is foreigners who have come to Europe," according to an English translation.
MIGRANT CRISIS PUSHES ITALY TO RESTORE BORDER CHECKS WITH SPAIN, TESTING EUROPE'S OPEN-BORDER SYSTEM
While not singling out Denmark's integrated immigrant population, she continued, "It is Hamas supporters. It is people who commit terror against European societies. It is people who do not recognize our fundamental European values. It is people who sympathize with some of the darkest forces in this world. So, Europe is threatened. The problem is that we are threatened both from outside and now from within, but it is not because of a disagreement between the Danish and Spanish governments, but because of people with an Islamic background who do not want the open, free European society, unfortunately."
Sweden-based foreign policy expert and author Daniel Schatz told Fox News Digital, "What is striking is not that a conservative politician is talking about illegal immigration, failed integration and Islamist extremism, it is that one of Europe’s leading center-left prime ministers is saying it in such blunt terms. That tells you how far the European immigration debate has shifted."
PORTUGAL ENACTS 'BURQA LAW' LARGELY PROHIBITING FACE COVERINGS IN PUBLIC
Frederiksen came to power in Denmark’s 2019 elections on what Reuters called a "platform of radical reforms to reach climate targets, lowering the pension age for manual workers - and stricter migration policies." Denmark already had some of the strongest asylum laws in Europe before 2019, including a 2018 law targeting "parallel societies." That law allowed the government to "demolish or sell off social housing areas where more than half of residents are from a ‘non-Western’ background," if certain criteria were met, and refugees in those areas are not eligible for family reunion.
In 2021, Frederiksen introduced a new deportation law allowing for refugees to be returned to their country of origin, if Denmark deemed it safe, even if Denmark had no diplomatic relations with that country, and even as the European Commission deemed Danish legislation on transferring asylum seekers to third countries while their claims were processed "incompatible with EU law."
Since June, Frederiksen has been a leading voice in opposition to the immigration policies of Spain’s Pedro Sánchez, telling Parliament, "It is no secret that I and the Spanish Prime Minister deeply disagree on immigration policy… I and we will not accept that Danish society has to pay the price for decisions in Spain that we fundamentally disagree with."
On Aug. 1, Frederiksen joined conservative Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and 20 other EU government leaders in a letter saying the EU "cannot allow mass crossings, the instrumentalization of migration or other hybrid threats to create the perception that illegal entry into the European Union is possible."
ITALY-SPAIN BORDER FEUD EXPOSES EUROPE’S DEEPENING IMMIGRATION DIVIDE
The two, currently the only female heads of government in the EU, followed that letter with an Aug. 10 joint statement saying they "are both proud of Europe’s Christian cultural heritage and we want to protect it. We expect that those who arrive in our countries and choose to make Europe their home respect our values and do not try to impose ways of life that we do not share. We believe that this is the right path to protect Europe and our common values. And we believe that millions of Europeans share this conviction."
Emma Schubart of the Henry Jackson Society told Fox News Digital, "Frederiksen is right to name the ‘enemy within’. Europe has spent years pretending that uncontrolled migration and failed integration come without consequences. They do not… Parallel societies have taken root, Islamist extremism has been allowed to fester and support for groups such as Hamas is no longer confined to the margins. Denmark understands the cost."
Daniel Schatz said Frederiksen "is essentially arguing that Europe faces threats from two directions: Russia from outside and anti-democratic extremism from within. For a center-left European leader, that is remarkably strong language." He noted Frederiksen’s "political formula has been straightforward: protect Denmark’s generous system of public benefits and social services, control the border and deny the populist right a monopoly on immigration. For an American audience, that is probably the most important thing to understand about the Danish model."
Frederiksen’s position is important, he said, because she did not move politically "because Danish voters suddenly became concerned about immigration. She moved because she realized years ago that many of them already were." He added, "The important distinction is that this is not an argument that immigrants are inherently criminal. It is an argument that a democratic society must be willing to confront failed integration when it occurs."

Schubart added, "Other leaders now need to show the same courage, secure their borders, deport those with no right to remain and make clear that integration into our laws and values is not optional."

title: AI firefighting drones take aim at wildfires
text:
Wildfires can get a frightening head start. A small ignition in remote terrain can grow while firefighters are still trying to reach it. Now, a new generation of AI firefighting drones could help shrink that response window.
CAL FIRE recently tested Seneca's autonomous suppression drones in California. Meanwhile, teams competing in the $11 million XPRIZE Wildfire competition put other autonomous systems through field testing in Alaska. The goal is to detect a fire early and get suppressant onto it while it is still small.
The timing is important. NOAA says human-caused warming is contributing to larger and more severe wildfires in California and the western United States. Research has also linked warming conditions with longer wildfire seasons in the West.
Here's how these firefighting drones work, what recent tests revealed and where they could be deployed next.
AMERICA’S FIREFIGHTER SHORTAGE HITS CRISIS LEVEL AS EMERGENCY CALLS TRIPLE, PUTTING LIVES AT RISK

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.
Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com.
CAL FIRE puts autonomous firefighting drones to the test
On July 15, CAL FIRE worked with the nonprofit FireWERX and engineers from California-based Seneca on a field test of autonomous firefighting drones. Five aircraft took part in the demonstration. CAL FIRE Deputy Chief Jack Worden said the technology could help firefighters who often attack small vegetation fires with backpack pumps and hand tools.
Seneca is designing its aircraft to respond quickly after crews identify a possible fire. The company's current system uses onboard sensors with AI and computer vision to help locate a fire. It can then deliver aerated Class A foam onto a targeted area. Seneca says its full systems use four to six drones and can deliver between 500 and 1,000 pounds of suppression capacity per trip.
One important point is that the payload figures can sound confusing. Reports from the CAL FIRE demonstration described the amount of water carried by individual drones and the volume of foam produced after mixing. Seneca's current product page instead describes suppression capacity by weight. Its Aspen deployment materials use yet another measure, finished foam volume. Those figures should not be treated as interchangeable.
These drones are designed for the first minutes of a fire
Seneca's aircraft cannot match the payload of a large airtanker. CAL FIRE already operates more than 70 fixed-wing and rotary-wing aircraft. The agency says that the fleet can reach many remote fires within its State Responsibility Area in about 20 minutes.
Smaller drones could serve a different purpose. Seneca says its aircraft can be transported by utility vehicles or positioned near areas with high fire risk. The system is being developed for jobs that include early attack, nighttime operations and work in difficult terrain. That could matter when a fire starts somewhere that ground crews cannot reach quickly.
San Bernardino County Fire tested an earlier Seneca Argo-1 system in December 2025. The county described that aircraft as semi-autonomous and said it used thermal tracking with precision targeting for early wildfire response. That description also highlights an important detail about the word "autonomous." The aircraft can handle substantial parts of the flight and targeting process on their own. However, the systems still operate under human supervision. For Aspen's planned deployment, Seneca says a single pilot will be able to oversee multiple aircraft.
DOORDASH GETS FAA APPROVAL FOR ITS OWN DELIVERY DRONES
Alaska test pushes autonomous firefighting further
A different firefighting system faced its own challenge in Alaska. XPRIZE held finals testing for its Autonomous Wildfire Response Track near Nenana, Alaska during June 2026. Three finalist teams had to use autonomous technology to detect and suppress early-stage fires without human intervention. Judges evaluated factors including speed, accuracy and suppression effectiveness.
One of those finalists was German company Dryad Networks. Dryad combines its Silvanet detection network with a drone system called Silvaguard. Silvanet uses solar-powered environmental sensors placed in forests. These sensors monitor combustion gases and particulates associated with the earliest stages of a fire. They communicate through Dryad's network, so a potential ignition can trigger a response. That wording is important because the sensors are doing more than looking for visible smoke.
How Dryad's system responds to a fire
Once Silvanet identifies a possible fire, a Silvaguard observation drone can launch automatically. The aircraft uses infrared and optical imaging to locate the source and determine whether there is an actual fire. A separate suppression drone can then respond to the confirmed location.
Dryad says its suppression drone can carry up to 100 liters of fire suppressant. That works out to about 26 gallons. The company has also demonstrated an observation drone that launches from a solar-powered hangar. In a November 2025 demonstration, Dryad said its system detected a controlled fire and extinguished it in under 12 minutes without human involvement.
During the XPRIZE finals in Alaska, Dryad says its sensors detected a small fire and triggered an autonomous response. The Silvaguard system then located and attacked the fire.
Aspen plans to bring firefighting drones into the field
Controlled tests can show what the technology is capable of. Real fire operations will be a much tougher test. Aspen Fire Protection District in Colorado has already signed a five-year, multimillion-dollar agreement with Seneca.
The agreement calls for a five-aircraft Seneca Strike Team and a mobile operations base. Seneca says the system has a capacity of about 500 gallons of finished foam per sortie. One pilot can oversee multiple aircraft because of the system's autonomy features. Seneca announced that the system would be delivered during summer 2026. For now, the contract represents one of the clearest moves from demonstration toward real-world deployment. The company also said Aspen firefighters would train on the aircraft before incorporating them into operations.
MISSOURI TESTS MEDICAL DRONES TO SPEED UP RURAL HEALTH CARE
California already uses AI to spot fires earlier
Firefighting drones could eventually work alongside technology that California already uses for earlier detection. CAL FIRE works with UC San Diego's ALERTCalifornia program, which operated more than 1,200 cameras and sensor arrays as of February 2026. The program says its AI wildfire system detected more than 1,200 fires during its first season. It also beat the first 911 report more than 30% of the time.
I've previously covered how Google's FireSat project uses specialized satellites and AI to spot wildfires earlier. That project has also taken a major step forward. Earth Fire Alliance launched the first three operational FireSat satellites on July 7, 2026. However, the system is still ramping up. The organization says operational data should begin reaching its Early Adopters at least twice daily during the fourth quarter of 2026.
Eventually, systems like FireSat and ALERTCalifornia could help spot an ignition. A nearby drone could then give firefighters another way to respond quickly. That connection is still developing, but it shows where wildfire technology may be headed.
What this means to you
If you live in a wildfire-prone area, these drones could eventually give local fire agencies another way to respond during the earliest stage of a fire. However, they have real limitations. Their payloads are far smaller than those of major firefighting aircraft. Their performance also depends on weather, terrain and safe coordination with other aircraft.
In addition, autonomous firefighting technology is still moving from demonstrations into real operations. You should continue to rely on official emergency alerts and evacuation instructions. Know how you would leave your neighborhood if conditions change. Also, keep important documents somewhere you can reach quickly.
The promise of these drones comes down to time. If they can reach a remote ignition while it is still small, firefighters may gain another opportunity to stop it before it becomes much harder to control.
Kurt's key takeaways
What interests me most about this technology is the focus on those first critical minutes. A drone will not replace a large airtanker. It also will not replace the judgment of experienced firefighters. Where I see potential is in getting suppression onto a remote fire faster. If a drone can slow a new ignition until more resources arrive, that could give crews an advantage they do not have today. Still, controlled demonstrations only tell us so much. The bigger test comes when these aircraft face unpredictable winds, active fire traffic and rapidly changing conditions. Fire agencies will also need clear procedures for coordinating autonomous systems with the people already working in the air and on the ground. That is when we will learn how valuable this technology can really be.

"Flooding may occur in poor drainage and urban areas."

It added, "The National Park Service wants visitors to have a memorable national park experience and get home safely and without injury. Visitor safety is our top priority, and we urge the public to stay aware of changing weather conditions."

"Those flash flood alerts are no joke."

title: Camp Mystic pulls plan to reopen this summer after backlash from grieving families
text:
Camp Mystic announced Thursday it will not reopen its facility for the summer 2026 season, marking a major shift in recovery plans following a catastrophic flood that killed 27 people last year.
Officials said the tragedy left 25 campers and two counselors dead at the all-girls Christian camp in Hill Country, Texas. Director Richard Eastland also died during separate rescue efforts, according to the family-owned camp.
The camp’s decision to drop its bid to reopen in May comes just days after the director broke down in a tearful apology at a state hearing that drew an outcry from lawmakers and grieving families over the effort to resume operations, according to the Associated Press (AP).
In a statement, leaders said they would rather not pursue another season than risk causing further harm to the affected families.
CAMP MYSTIC DIRECTOR DIES WHILE TRYING TO SAVE KIDS DURING TEXAS FLOODING
"No administrative process or summer season should move forward while families continue to grieve," the camp said.
"This decision is intended to remove any doubt that Camp Mystic has heard the concerns expressed by grieving families, members of the Texas House and Senate investigating committees and citizens across our state. Respect for those voices requires that we step back now."
REPUBLICAN CONGRESSMAN REUNITES WITH DAUGHTERS AFTER TEXAS CAMP FLOODING, THANKS ‘COUNTLESS HEROES’
They further expressed their sympathy for everyone impacted by last year’s disaster, adding that they understand there is nothing they can do to reverse the damage or ease the pain caused.
"Twenty-eight precious lives were lost. We recognize that no statement and no decision can undo that loss or ease the burden carried each day by parents, siblings, loved ones, survivors, first responders and our beautiful Kerr County community. We also recognize that over 800 girls want to return to Camp Mystic Cypress Lake this summer. Our special bond with our Camp Mystic families does not change or end with the announcement," the statement read.
Owners of the camp previously said they hoped to reopen in late May, expecting 900 attendees, and were planning to use only parts of the facility that did not flood, The AP reported.
The plans subsequently sparked significant outrage from victims’ families and some prominent officials, who urged regulators to deny the camp’s license, which was under review by the Texas Department of State Health Services.

title: Camp Mystic leaders prioritized equipment, told children to 'shelter in place' as flooding closed in: lawsuit
text:
Families of six girls who died in flooding at Camp Mystic filed a wrongful death lawsuit alleging camp leaders ignored mounting warnings and delayed evacuations, keeping the youngest campers in low-lying cabins near the overflowing Guadalupe River.
The lawsuit, filed in the Travis County District Court, alleges negligence and gross negligence, including failure to maintain and follow flood evacuation plans, failure to move children to higher ground once flooding began, inadequate training and communication systems, and operating children’s cabins in floodplains despite the known risk.
The suit says forecasters began flagging risk on July 3, citing a National Weather Service Flood Watch and Flood Advisories, but the camp failed to take proactive steps to prevent tragedy.
911 CALLS, POLICE REPORT DETAILS DARK TIMELINE TO ARIZONA GIRL'S TRAGIC DEATH
On July 4, the fateful night when floodwaters overtook the girl’s camp, the lawsuit alleges that Camp Mystic leaders met with grounds staff to secure equipment rather than awake the young children and bring them to immediate safety.
At 2 a.m., the Kerr County Sheriff’s Office logged its first emergency call about hazardous conditions. At 2:10 a.m., counselors reported cabins taking on water and, according to the complaint, were told to shelter in place with counselors "not allowed" phones, radios or walkie-talkies.
Counselors who were awake began moving girls toward a hillside around 3 a.m., with accounts of a broader evacuation at 3:11 a.m., the lawsuit says.
FLOODS, LANDSLIDES IN MEXICO LEAVE AT LEAST 41 DEAD
Photos timestamped 3:26 a.m. show campers still able to walk toward higher ground as water rose across the property. By about 3:44 a.m., doors were "breaking open" and water rushed in, the lawsuit says.
Apple Watch data from leaders allegedly recorded submersion at 3:51 a.m. and 4:09 a.m. An emergency call from the camp was logged at 3:59 a.m.
The families say the youngest girls were kept in Bubble Inn and Twins I & Twins II on "the flats" near the river even as water rose, despite nearby options: a hillside roughly 20 yards from Bubble Inn and a two-story commissary with exterior stairs near the Twins cabins. Staff members who lived above the commissary survived, the suit says.
The lawsuit includes a one-page "Emergency Instructions" sheet that told campers to stay inside during floods and stated, "All cabins are constructed on high, safe ground." Families call this guidance "false and dangerous." The document was allegedly recovered from a counselor’s trunk after the flood.
The six families of the young girls argue the camp sits in a FEMA-mapped flood hazard area in a region along the Guadalupe known as "Flood Alley," citing federal maps that place cabins in the floodway and floodplains and prior major floods in 1932, 1952, 1978 and 1987. FEMA identified the site as a Special Flood Hazard Area in 2011, the suit says.
The lawsuit names the girls as Virginia "Wynne" Naylor and Jane "Janie" Hunt, both housed in Bubble Inn; Lucy Lee Dillon and Kellyanne Elizabeth Lytal, housed in Twins I; and Hadley Rebecca Hanna and Virginia Larins Hollis, housed in Twins II.
All were 8 or 9, according to the filing. They were among 27 campers and counselors who died in the flooding.
In a statement to Fox News Digital, Camp Mystic said that they are "continuing to pray for the grieving families and ask for God's healing and comfort."
"We empathize with the families of the campers and counselors and all families in the Hill Country who lost loved ones in the horrific and unprecedented flood of July 4," Jeff Ray, legal counsel for Camp Mystic, said in a statement to Fox News Digital.
"We intend to demonstrate and prove that this sudden surge of floodwaters far exceeded any previous flood in the area by several magnitudes, that it was unexpected and that no adequate warning systems existed in the area. We disagree with several accusations and misinformation in the legal filings regarding the actions of Camp Mystic and Dick Eastland, who lost his life as well. We will thoroughly respond to these accusations in due course," he said.

title: Families sue Camp Mystic over deadly Texas flood, allege negligence and profit motive
text:
Families of seven girls and camp counselors killed in the July 4 Camp Mystic flood in Hunt, Texas, have filed a wrongful death and negligence lawsuit, alleging the camp’s owners ignored flood risks and state safety rules to protect profits.
The lawsuit, filed Nov. 10 in Travis County District Court by attorney R. Paul Yetter of Yetter Coleman LLP, names the families of Anna Margaret Bellows, Lila Bonner, Chloe Childress, Molly DeWitt, Katherine Ferruzzo, Lainey Landry and Blakely McCrory — all of whom died in the catastrophic flooding.
The 75-page petition claims Camp Mystic and its owners "put profit over safety" and "chose to house young girls in flood-prone areas to avoid the cost of relocating cabins." It also accuses the camp of failing to create or follow an evacuation plan, despite state regulations requiring one.
"Just such a tragedy hit our State on July 4, 2025," the lawsuit reads. "When 25 campers and two counselors needlessly and tragically died in the floodwaters at Camp Mystic."
CAMP MYSTIC MAKES CONTROVERSIAL DECISION ABOUT FUTURE OF TEXAS CAMP WHERE 27 DIED IN FLOODING
Camp Mystic spans 725 acres along the Guadalupe River in the Texas Hill Country, an area long known for deadly flash floods. The filing cites a 1990 interview with then-director Richard Eastland, who reportedly told the Austin-American Statesman, "I’m sure there will be other drownings. People don’t heed the warnings."
According to the lawsuit, the camp ignored multiple warnings — from weather alerts, staff concerns, and its own experience. Counselors allegedly pleaded to evacuate girls from low-lying cabins but were told to "stay put because that’s the plan."
TIMELINE DETAILED IN THE LAWSUIT:
• 1:14 a.m. — National Weather Service issued a "life-threatening flash flood" warning.
• 1:45 a.m.–2:13 a.m. — Camp leaders Richard and Edward Eastland allegedly worked to move equipment instead of ordering an evacuation.
• 2:20 a.m. — Counselors reported water entering cabins but were instructed to remain inside.

• 3:35–3:51 a.m. — Richard Eastland’s SUV was swept away as he tried to rescue girls from Bubble Inn; all 13 campers and two counselors in that cabin drowned.

CAMP MYSTIC DIRECTOR DIES WHILE TRYING TO SAVE KIDS DURING TEXAS FLOOD
The petition argues that the girls could have safely evacuated within 60 seconds to higher ground if not ordered to remain in their cabins.
Families accuse Camp Mystic of gross negligence, premises liability, and intentional infliction of emotional distress. The filing also highlights a written policy stating: "In case of flood, all campers on Senior Hill must stay in their cabins... All cabins are constructed on safe, high locations."
The lawsuit also alleges that camp administrators misled families after the disaster, telling them the girls were merely "unaccounted for" hours after the floodwaters receded.
Adding to families’ anger, the lawsuit cites the camp’s decision to announce its reopening for the next summer season while one camper, Cile Steward, remained missing.
